title: Comment on: Why were Victorian elites so effective?
body:

> There is a longstanding view that the prosperity of Britain’s elites came at the cost of the hundreds of millions whom they subordinated and oppressed, and no doubt that is at least partly true. But on their own terms, the British ruling class enjoyed a victorious century.
> Maybe the Victorian elite succeeded in spite of being feckless and incompetent: the Industrial Revolution created great wealth, which they enjoyed passively and parasitically. We cannot run controlled experiments on Victorian Britain, so this thesis is hard to test. But I want to explore the possibility that a relentless focus on soft skills, team building, and intra-elite networking actually worked rather well.
The essay is intentionally exploring an alternative to the obvious one. I think the essay does brush off the cruelty of the empire too quickly, but cruelty isn’t inherently profitable, so there’s still some explaining to do.

title: Comment on: Shipping JPEG XL in Chrome
body:
> Apple refused to support it because they wanted to patent-laden alternative to thrive.
Where do people get this stuff?
Apple finally supported WebP in 2020, 10 years after it was released by Google. Firefox added WebP support in 2019, a year before Safari. Was Mozilla also part of conspiracy to undermine WebP? Come on now.
Seems to me neither Apple or Mozilla wanted to be forced to support a format they had no say in developing. Usually there's a process for coming to consensus on standards.
WebP is ubiquitous now, not the case in 2010 when it was released.
It had advantages compared to JPEG, but not enough at the time to justify changing workflows, etc. WebP initially had better compression than JPEG, but as encoders/decoders improved (MozJPEG, Jpegli, turbo-libjpeg, Guetzli) the lead WebP had mostly went away regarding compression and visual fidelity.
Going forward, WebP is becoming less relevant by the day; it doesn't support wide gamut color; it only supports RGB. It's max pixel count is quite limited compared to AVIF and JPEG XL. Newer formats have use cases beyond the web; WebP doesn't.

title: Ask HN: Is this the beginning of the end of open source?
body:
If you're following the photopea incident, I'm sure you'd concur that the writing was on the wall. It's an inevitable outcome of the rise of AI in software dev. Any project that sees a semblance of success will be cloned overnight many times over and will find itself competing with its own copies.
We saw glimpses of a similar situation in the past when large cloud platforms cloned popular softwares in a not a very dissimilar manner. This led to the creation of "source available" as an alternative to open source that gained some traction of its own. But since this mostly affected a few large players, open source by and itself was large unaffected still supported by large volumes of individuals driven by passion, motivated towards their craft.
The concept of open source is itself something of an anomaly not seen in any other industry or at any other time in history. Partly fueled by an individual's desire to exhibit original work, and partly supported by the fact that code needs someone of an equal to work with, it still allowed authors to reap a net benefit while giving out their IP for free. LLMs have turned that picture over completely. It's not only trivial to derive, for all purposes, an exact copy of the IP while obscuring the source, it's also possible to maintain and operate the IP with a relatively low bar of expertise. But the other inconspicuous problem brought about by LLMs is that can you even claim original work any more? When no one believes that you wrote it yourself, what motivation remains to continue publishing as open source? With no net benefit to revealing your IP, will we see a revival to closed source distribution again?

title: Comment on: Why were Victorian elites so effective?
body:
My hypothesis:
1. Empires do not generate wealth, they cost wealth. Or rather they do not generate an economic surplus (the wealth available to the central government via taxation that can be used for whatever the government/elites want). A nation of 10 million will have more economic wealth than a nation of one million, but most of that is needed to keep the 10 million alive and to maintain the infrastructure and pay the local police to keep everyone in line, etc -- only a small fraction of total wealth can be effectively taxed by the empire and spent on arbitrary stuff like increasing the size of the Navy. That is what I mean by surplus.
A nation starts out with an economic surplus (here, I mean a real surplus, not a surplus of silver, but of real wealth) and they use that surplus to get a big army and go conquering. And each time they conquer, a part of that surplus is expended until they reach their maximum extent.
If this was not the case, we'd have a one world government, where the bigger you get, the bigger your surplus and no one can compete with you. But that is not what we see, what we see is that empires expand until they can't afford to keep expanding. Why did England give up its colonies? Because after WW2 it had too many war debts and couldn't keep subsidizing those colonies -- they were too expensive to keep. Same reason for why Rome stopped expanding and had so many financial problems. The check on empire is always bankruptcy. You can look at the trillions the US spends on foreign wars, which far exceeds the economic benefit we get of waging those wars. You can argue, for example, that we got some oil from Iraq, but we still have to pay for that oil, so whatever discount we got on oil comes nowhere near the cost of invading and administering Iraq. That is how all empires work -- France was always better off, financially, just paying market rate for whatever minerals it could get in Africa than the massive resources it spent on trying to control and…

title: Comment on: Meta and Microsoft take steps to reduce employee usage of Claude AI
body:
> My company took away my Claude because it’s too expensive.
My company didn't took away any expensive model, but it did imposed a tight budget and gave my team hardware to run local models. The budget works mainly as an influence on the decision process of which model to run. We can still run expensive budget-burning models if we really want to, but there is a clear incentive to use options that allow us to save our token budget for a rainy prompt.
Surprisingly, I feel this had a positive impact on results. Instead of succumbing to extremely expensive one-shot prompts with the most expensive model in the news, chaining agents running cheap models equiped with context and specialized skills and scripts ends up having a better and more reliable output. And faster too.
I think there is a lot of propaganda, perhaps even astroturfing, on how only the most expensive models churned out by US companies are worth using. Nowadays the cheapest models get the job done, and local models can already handle most tasks as well specially as part of orchestration chains.

But it's missing the point: it is not always about "better" or "worse".
And in fact humans are special in a very straight-forward way: we share one thing with each other that no AI will share with us, which is our common biological ancestry and its consequences.
So, when looking at a human-made painting - which could look much worse than flawless AI counterpart - I'm not just looking at a painting, but I'm also thinking about what it took to produce, how much the artist was struggling to balance the need of survival with the need to create, how big was the price they had to pay, how it's similar or different to my own life, whether I'd be willing to pay such a price, and a lot more.

Hi HN!
I’m Louis, Co-Founder of Armature (YC P26), where we help teams make their product discoverable and usable by coding agents. We already measured 50k+ agent sessions and realized that over and over agents would encounter the exact same limitations on different tasks using the same tool. So we wondered why these weren’t fixed. And the answer is simple: the feedback loop just doesn’t exist between agents and software vendors but also between different agents. Humans can share their experience on platforms like https://g2.com and https://trustpilot.com, but agents have nowhere to.
So we created: https://agent.reviews: the G2 for agents.
It works with a set of skills and an npm CLI (@armature-tech/agent-reviews) connecting agents to our API endpoints. Anyone can ask their agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, etc.) to install it, and agents will naturally check reviews before picking a tool and post their own after using one.
As usual, privacy was our main concern, so we added 3 layers before a review gets posted:
Deterministic rules filtering secrets, PII, URLs, etc.
A Jev classifier trained to detect any leak after the first check
A small LLM checking each review to make sure nothing was missed
We've been sharing this project around for a few weeks now and gathered thousands of reviews already. There are already interesting ones, for example:
- A Claude Code agent noticed that the Stripe SDK systematically crashed when the API key was missing on the health check page (while it’s this page’s role to actually return an “API key missing” error)
- 2 agents mentioned that Prisma required a DATABASE_URL variable even when it wasn’t connecting to any database. They both put fake URLs as a workaround, and it worked.
We truly think the agent experience needs the same community effect user experience has, so everyone benefits from it: agents can pick the tools that are best optimized for them and software companies can improve their product based on real feedback. That’s wh…

title: Tonbridge & Malling Borough Council: ITT TMBC - Cemetery Management Software
body:
Tonbridge & Malling Borough Council is out to market for a new digital software solution for managing the records of Tonbridge Cemetery. 
Located on Shipbourne Road, close to Tonbridge town centre, Tonbridge Cemetery was established in 1858 and has served the local community for more than 160 years. The cemetery includes historic chapel buildings dating from the 1860s, mature, landscaped grounds, and a memorial garden that provides a peaceful setting for the interment and remembrance of cremated remains.
Covering approximately 14 hectares (34.6 acres), Tonbridge Cemetery is one of the borough's largest and most historic public open spaces. With around 14,000 grave spaces, the cemetery reflects generations of local history and continues to provide an important place of remembrance for residents and visitors alike. 
Historically, cemetery records were maintained through handwritten registers, burial books, and paper plans. To improve efficiency and accessibility, a digital cemetery management system was introduced in 2002, enabling records to be digitised and managed electronically. 
A key requirement of any future system will be the ability to securely migrate all existing records, ensuring the continued preservation and accessibility of both historic and current cemetery data.

title: Allow editing Data Tables in Protected Environments (for environment-specific configurations)
body: **Problem** In Protected Environments (Settings → Environments → "Protected Environment" enabled), workflow editing is correctly disabled to enforce Git-based deployments. However, **Data Tables remain locked for manual edits**, even though their *content* (rows) is not version-controlled via Git—only metadata and column definitions are. This creates an inconsistency with **Credentials and Variables**, which *can* be edited in Protected Environments (as their Git stubs require environment-specific adjustments). Data Tables often serve similar purposes (e.g., storing environment-specific configurations like API endpoints, feature flags, or lookup values), and blocking manual edits forces workarounds like: * Temporarily disabling environment protection (risky) * Using external storage (e.g., databases) for what should be simple table data * Hardcoding values in workflows (less maintainable) **Proposed Solution** Allow manual editing of **Data Table rows** in Protected Environments, while keeping the table *schema* (columns, types) tied to Git deployments. This aligns with the existing behavior for Credentials/Variables and acknowledges that: 1. Data Table *content* is not part of Git deployments (only structure is). 2. Environment-specific data (e.g., prod-only configurations) must sometimes be added post-deployment. **Potential Concerns Addressed** * **Safety:** Row edits wouldn’t affect workflow logic (unlike workflow changes), and schema changes would still require Git. * *…

title: New app builder: app's git storage loads every loose object from S3 on each request, so a large repo takes down self-hosted backend pods
body: My goal: Keep using the new app builder on an actively developed React app without opening it in the builder taking down our backend pods. Ideally that means a supported way to pack or compact an app's git storage, or confirmation that packing or caching is planned. Issue: Opening one of our React apps in the new app builder overloaded both main-backend pods. They failed their liveness probes and Kubernetes restarted them at the same time, so users got 503s for about 4 minutes. The app's git storage in S3 is all loose objects and has never been packed: \[rr.git_storage\] Client created looseObjects=2615 packFiles=0 refs=66 \[rr.git_storage\] Loaded repo from blob storage looseCount=2615 looseBytes=2.6MB packCount=0 looseMs=22662 The effective git config disables housekeeping: gc.auto=0 maintenance.auto=false receive.unpacklimit=1000000 receive.autogc=false The app itself is only about 356 files (about 2 MB), so most of those objects are history: version history and builder branches. Each GET /api/ai/rr/git/v2/apps//files reloads the whole repo from S3, one GET per object, and nothing seems to be cached between requests. One load takes 7–13s. The builder sends several of these requests at once, and with 3–4 running on the same pod each took 22–56s. While that runs, the pod is too busy to answer /api/checkHealth, so the liveness probe kills it. The builder's retried requests then do the same to the other pod.
